# Workshop 10
 
 # Co-Creating with the Multi-Lingual Communities
 
 **Speakers:** [Ruthie Nachmany](https:/innovation.nj.gov/about/team/ruthie-nachmany) (Product Manager, NJ Office of Innovation), [Sofía Bosch Gómez](https:/burnes.northeastern.edu/people/sofia-bosch-gomez) (Assistant Professor, Northeastern University; Burns Center for Social Change), and [Anirudh Dinesh](https:/burnes.northeastern.edu/people/anirudh-dinesh) (Research Fellow, The GovLab)
 
 This workshop presents two complementary approaches to AI-powered multilingual engagement. Ruthie Nachmany describes New Jersey’s statewide language access work, including multilingual [government benefits communication](https:/github.com/newjersey/feedback-widget) , [an AI assistant](https:/innovation.nj.gov/projects/ai-assistant) , and a [feedback widget](https:/innovation.nj.gov/projects/feedback-widget) . Sofía Bosch Gómez and Anirudh Dinesh present [AIEP](https:/alpha.a-iep.org/about-the-project) (AI-powered Individualized Education Program), a tool that translates and simplifies special education documents for multilingual families.
 
 ## New Jersey language access work
 
 New Jersey serves diverse multilingual communities. Spanish speakers alone make up 95% of language access requests in the state’s unemployment cases. One call center agent observed: “A lot of the Spanish speakers are paying a third-party agency when they should be able to make a claim for free by themselves online.” The NJ Office of Innovation is developing a comprehensive language access approach that combines human expertise, AI tools, and continuous feedback loops.
 
 [The unemployment insurance modernization project](https:/innovation.nj.gov/blog/2025-08-08-translation) , a collaboration between NJDOL, the Office of Innovation, Nava, Truss, and [U.S. Digital Response](https:/www.usdigitalresponse.org/resources/social-safety-net-2-0-how-new-jersey-is-forging-a-new-path-with-language-access-and-generative-ai) , involved eight months of content co-creation. The team co-designed with bilingual frontline staff and UI subject matter experts, then validated with Spanish-speaking residents from 10 different countries. Four Spanish-bilingual UX researchers and content designers worked with 15 New Jersey residents who had direct experience navigating the system. The output included translated UI content plus a [general government benefits translation assistant](https:/usdr.gitbook.io/benefits-resource-hub/language-access/ai-translation-assistants-for-benefits-programs) , [a Spanish translation guide](https:/usdr.gitbook.io/benefits-resource-hub/language-access/spanish-translation-guide-for-benefits-programs) , and an unemployment [Spanish glossary](https:/www.nj.gov/labor/myunemployment/help/glossary/index_espanol.shtml) .
 
 [The results were significant.](https:/www.usdigitalresponse.org/resources/social-safety-net-2-0-how-new-jersey-is-forging-a-new-path-with-language-access-and-generative-ai) Form completion time dropped from over 3 hours to 28 minutes; parity was achieved between English and Spanish speakers; call center wait times fell from 40 minutes to 2 minutes; claims requiring manual review dropped 14%.
 
 New Jersey also built an [open-source feedback widget](https:/innovation.nj.gov/projects/feedback-widget) , now deployed on 13 state websites. It asks “Did you find what you were looking for?” with Yes/No buttons and an open response box. This drives quick changes: after feedback showed people couldn’t find what they needed, they added search functionality to [NJ.gov](http:/nj.gov) . Complaints dropped 30% within two weeks. Identity verification issues flagged through the widget led to targeted fixes. “Make it easy for people to tell you what’s working and what’s not,” said Nachmany.
 
 ## AIEP: Translating special education documents
 
 IEPs (Individualized Education Programs) are complex legal and medical documents, often 50+ pages, that parents need to understand to advocate for their children’s education. For non-English speakers, the barrier is high. Many families end up hiring education advocates to navigate the paperwork.
 
 [AIEP](https:/alpha.a-iep.org) , developed in partnership with Innovate Public Schools and supported by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and the Burnes Center for Social Change’s AI for Impact program, addresses this gap. It extracts text from PDF IEPs via OCR, redacts private information (addresses, SSNs) before any LLM processing, translates into Spanish, Chinese, or Vietnamese, simplifies into plain language, generates a glossary of technical terms, and provides structured summaries with “Know Your Rights” information.
 
 [This project was born from a distinctive co-design process.](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/designing-ai-with-communities-education) The team ran focus groups with Spanish-speaking parents in San Francisco and San Jose, starting in March 2025. They created two community leadership roles: Parent Leader Navigators, who receive extended training and master the platform to support other families, and Parent Leader Canvassers, who complete foundational training and contribute feedback through outreach. Both groups participate in ongoing focus groups to ensure the tool stays responsive to real needs.
 
 Some of the changes made in response to the community input:
 
 (1) Summary structure: Parents reported stress from documents that led with the diagnosis and problems. The team redesigned the summaries to start with the child’s strengths, then goals and services. Parents noticed the change immediately in the next focus group.
 
 (2) Linguistic sensitivity: The “Know Your Rights” section was initially translated into technically correct Spanish, but parents found it culturally aggressive. The language was toned down to avoid a combative tone.
 
 (3) Opening up the prompts: The team loaded prompts used to train the AI model into a Google Doc and shared it with parents and educators for feedback in any format. They engaged experts (both by training and lived experience) to identify terms the model should look for when processing IEPs. Plain language prompts let non-technical participants directly shape the AI output.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Reliability and guardrails
 
 LLM translation presents specific challenges that came up in both presentations. Models are non-deterministic, meaning the same input can produce slightly different outputs each time (unlike Google Translate). They also lack specialized domain expertise. They can soften legal language in ways that matter: “shall not be eligible” might become “may have reduced possibility,” and these nuances become critical for benefits eligibility. Quality varies by language, too. English, Spanish, and European languages are well-supported; regional languages are less robust.
 
 NJ shared a bit about their approach to this challenge. Research studies compared fine-tuned LLM translations with human translations, Google Translate, and unprompted LLMs. Fine-tuned LLM translations were nearly indistinguishable from expert translations. But the team emphasized keeping humans in the loop. Translations are tested for readability by end users and reviewed for accuracy by a competent human translator paired with a subject matter expert.
 
 The speakers also sketched a rough framework for thinking about risk:
 
 Lowest risk: Policy feedback, public engagement, outreach materials… Most room for experimentation. Errors are catchable, and consequences are limited.
 
 Medium risk: Co-designing services (like benefits programs). Requires human validation by translators and subject matter experts before anything goes live.
 
 Medium Risk: Co-designing AI tools (like IEP translators). Requires strong guardrails because the tool will operate at scale with less human review per interaction
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 The NJ case shows what happens when you tap into frontline staff expertise. Call center agents helped create the Spanish glossary because they knew the common roadblocks and how to explain concepts to real users. Nachmany said that “Staff who talk to the public daily are your critical source of insight.”
 
 The AIEP case shows what thorough co-design looks like. Sharing prompts in a Google Doc, letting parents flag terms the model should recognize, and redesigning outputs based on emotional response (not just comprehension or proficiency). This is an example of giving communities genuine input on how the AI works.
 
 Both projects treat imperfect-but-validated translation as better than English-only content with browser auto-translate, which is the de facto status quo in most government contexts.
 
 One framing from Dinesh worth noting: “I’m not obsessed with scale. The frustration was about reaching communities that don’t speak English or aren’t comfortable with text-based surveys.” So the goal isn’t necessarily more reach, but reaching people who are currently excluded.
